questions.statement: She says, 'My shift starts at six.' When does her work begin?
questions.context: In a Heredia hospital, a nurse announces when her morning shift begins.

options.feedback: Six in the morning matches the number she says and the morning context of a shift start.
Six at night needs the p.m. marker, and she never mentions evening, so this hour conflicts.
Four is a number the recording never uses, so this hour is invented rather than heard.
Nine belongs to the evening round of shifts, and she announces only one starting time.

questions.explanation:
A stated detail is confirmed by matching both the number and the time marker you hear, here six in the morning.

questions.statement: He says, 'We count from five and we finish at seven.' How long is it?
questions.context: At a Monteverde eco-lodge, a guide explains the morning bird count.

options.feedback: Half an hour would end at 5:30, and no such second time appears anywhere in what he says.
Seven minus five gives exactly two hours, and both times are stated, so the duration is certain.
Five is the hour the count starts, not its length, and confusing a start with a duration is a common slip.
Twelve hours would run past the evening, but the count is complete at seven, so this is far too long.

questions.explanation:
To infer a duration, subtract the earlier time from the later one: seven o'clock less five o'clock equals two hours.

questions.statement: He says, 'The bridge is closed and we drive around the hill.' What is the effect?
questions.context: In Alajuela, a bus driver explains why his morning trip takes longer now.

options.feedback: Driving around the hill adds distance rather than removing it, so a shorter route is the opposite of the truth.
Passenger numbers are never mentioned; the only changes he names are the closure and the new path.
Nothing is said about what he charges, so a fare increase is a guess added to the announcement.
A detour always adds kilometres and minutes, so the direct effect of his two facts is a longer trip.

questions.explanation:

questions.context: At a Cartago college fair, an admissions officer explains campus transport.

options.feedback: Two named departure times mean two runs a day, and the word only confirms that nothing else operates.
The word only rules out continuous service, so a shuttle running all morning contradicts what she announces.
No price or fee appears in her description, so a noon charge is invented rather than heard.

questions.context: In a Puntarenas harbour talk, a captain explains when the boats leave.

options.feedback: Three never appears in the announcement, so the only figures on offer are four and the rejected five.
He states four and explicitly rejects five, so four is the sailing time a traveller should trust.
Five is the hour he refuses with the word not, so picking it repeats the error he corrected.
Six is not mentioned at all in what he says, so it cannot be the departure time he announced.

questions.explanation:
A correction with not still carries information: the rejected option is the wrong one and the retained hour is the right one.

questions.context: In a Liberia town meeting, a resident complains about noise from a nearby bar.

options.feedback: She never says the music is quiet; her complaint is about how long the disturbance lasts, not about volume.
She describes noise carrying on, not a bar shutting down, so an early closing is not what she reports.
The width of the street never comes up; her details are the music, the cars and the hour of ten.
Music stopping at ten while cars keep arriving means the noise lasts past that hour, which is the real problem.

questions.explanation:
When a speaker joins two facts with but, the surprising half carries the message: the music stops, yet the noise goes on.

options.text: The truck enters at any hour.
options.feedback: Entering at any hour ignores the closing time she reads aloud, so it breaks the rule she announced.

options.text: The truck pays a late fee.
options.feedback: No payment or fee appears in the notice, so a late charge is an invented consequence of her words.
She names a single gate; a second gate used as a workaround is not part of what she read.

options.feedback: Full support needs firmer praise, yet his hedged phrase raises the idea only to question it.

options.text: He has no opinion at all.
options.feedback: Raising a habit without praise is not neutrality; the hedge and his topic point to a reservation.

options.text: He doubts it is the best choice.
options.feedback: A careful academic hedge such as some usually signals doubt, so he is questioning solo work, not backing it.
He issues no rule at all in what he says, so turning his doubt into a ban misreads his tone.

questions.explanation:
Hedged phrases like some or a few signal the speaker's doubt, so listeners must infer the attitude and not only the topic.

questions.context: In a Quevedo museum talk, a guide says the museum closes at six.

options.feedback: Nine is never mentioned as a closing hour, so this would replace one wrong word with another wrong word.

Removing the line throws away correct information when only one word inside it is inaccurate.

questions.statement: She says: dig the rows, add compost, then sow the seed. Which order is it?
questions.context: In a Guapiles interview, a farmer explains how she plants coffee on her farm.

options.text: Dig the rows, add compost, then sow.
options.feedback: She prepares the ground, feeds it and sows last, and that is exactly the fixed sequence she described.

options.text: Add compost, dig the rows, then sow.
options.feedback: The ground has to be dug before compost goes in, so putting compost first breaks the order she gave.

options.text: Dig the rows, sow, then add compost.
options.feedback: Compost is added before sowing, not after it, so this list reverses the middle two steps.

options.text: Sow the seed, dig the rows, then compost.
options.feedback: Nothing can be sown before the rows are dug and fed, so this arrangement starts with the last real step.

questions.explanation:
Listening for a sequence means catching the order words she uses: first, then and only then mark the true chain of actions.

questions.context: In a Turrialba interview, a man explains why he changed jobs last year.

options.feedback: He rules the pay explanation out with the word not, so choosing money reverses the reason he kept.
Working hours are never mentioned; the contrast he draws is between boredom and low pay.
His supervisor is not part of the interview, so an unfair boss is a detail the recording never supplies.
He names boredom as his reason and rejects money, so this option matches the cause he actually stressed.

questions.explanation:
When a speaker contrasts two causes with not, the reason he keeps is the true one and the other is a trap for inattentive listeners.

questions.statement: One of them came while it rained. Which summary adds nothing she said?
questions.context: In a Palmares interview, a shopkeeper counts three customers in her morning.

options.text: She waited for three rainy customers.
options.feedback: This makes the customers wait and ties all three to the rain, two details she never mentions in the interview.

options.text: Three customers came in, one while it rained.
options.feedback: It keeps the three customers and the rainy hour exactly as heard, without adding a cause, a feeling or a total.

options.text: She served nobody during the rain.
options.feedback: One rainy customer is the opposite of nobody in the rain, so this summary contradicts the recording.

options.text: Her shop was busy all morning.
options.feedback: Three customers and one slow hour do not make a busy morning, so this overstates what the recording shows.

questions.explanation:
A faithful summary keeps the heard detail and refuses to add causes, moods or quantities that the speaker never supplied.

options.feedback: A one-hour forecast gives a duration, but the host is warning about danger, not only about timing.

questions.statement: Note: 'training - moved - 4 p.m.' Which sentence reports it correctly?
questions.context: In a Heredia interview, a coach explains that he moved his training session.

options.text: Training moves from four in the morning.
options.feedback: The note gives no starting time and says morning nowhere, so an early shift is invented detail.

options.text: Training was moved to four in the afternoon.
options.feedback: A single afternoon at four o'clock matches a passive report of a change, the normal way to note a new time.

options.text: Training will move to four tomorrow.

options.text: Training was moved from four in the afternoon.
options.feedback: The note records the new time rather than the old one, so reporting it as a time left behind reverses the change.

Turning shorthand into a full sentence needs the missing pieces: a time, an afternoon marker and a passive verb for a finished change.
